Unit 2: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
Unit 3: Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions
Unit 4: Inference for Quantitative Data: Means

terms.def: Two categorical variables are associated when the distribution of one differs across the categories of the other, for example when the percent who ride the bus differs between class years. Equal percents in every group mean no association.
terms.topicTitle: Tabular and Graphical Representations for the Distributions of Two Categorical Variables

terms.def: Phrases that set a boundary on a count or measurement: at least k (<math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo>≥</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ge k</annotation></semantics></math>), at most k or no more than k (<math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\le k</annotation></semantics></math>), more than k (<math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo>></mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">> k</annotation></semantics></math>), fewer than k (<math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo><</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">< k</annotation></semantics></math>), no fewer than k (<math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo>≥</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ge k</annotation></semantics></math>). For counts, fewer than k is the same as at most <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k - 1</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Inequalities in Words

terms.def: A graph of a categorical variable with one bar per category, separated by gaps, whose height (from 0) is the category’s count or relative frequency.
terms.topicTitle: Graphical Representations for One Categorical Variable

terms.def: A sampling method is biased if it systematically overestimates or underestimates the population value, in the same direction sample after sample.
terms.topicTitle: Potential Problems with Sampling

terms.def: In a binomial setting, the binomial random variable X counts the successes in the n trials. Its distribution, the binomial distribution with parameters n and p, gives <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(X = k)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac linethickness="0"><mi>n</mi><mi>k</mi></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><msup><mi>p</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>p</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \binom{n}{k}p^k(1 - p)^{n - k}</annotation></semantics></math> for <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>…</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k = 0, 1, \dots, n</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: The Binomial Distribution

terms.def: A binomial setting is a chance process with a fixed number n of trials, each with two outcomes (success or failure), trials independent of each other, and the same probability of success p on every trial.
terms.topicTitle: The Binomial Distribution

terms.def: Keeping subjects (single-blind) or both subjects and the people who interact with them or measure the response (double-blind) from knowing who received which treatment.
terms.topicTitle: Experimental Design

terms.def: A graph of the five-number summary: a box from <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_1</annotation></semantics></math> to <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_3</annotation></semantics></math> with a line at the median, whiskers to the most extreme values inside the <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.5</mn><mo>×</mo><mtext>IQR</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.5 \times \text{IQR}</annotation></semantics></math> fences, and outliers drawn as separate points.
terms.topicTitle: Graphical Representations of Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

terms.def: A variable whose values place each unit in a group or category, such as eye color or yes and no. Numbers used as labels, like ZIP codes, are categorical.
terms.topicTitle: Variables

terms.def: A cause-and-effect conclusion says that changing the explanatory variable changes the response. It needs an experiment in which chance decides who gets which condition; observational studies cannot rule out confounding.
terms.topicTitle: The Investigative Question Revisited and Data Collection

terms.def: A study that collects data from every member of the population.
terms.topicTitle: The Investigative Question Revisited and Data Collection

terms.def: A typical or middle value of a distribution, around which the data are located.
terms.topicTitle: Descriptions for One Quantitative Variable Distributions

terms.def: The Central Limit Theorem says that when the sample size n is large, the sampling distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal, whatever the shape of the population. A common guide is n of 30 or more; if the population is normal, <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{x}</annotation></semantics></math> is normal for any n.
terms.topicTitle: Sampling Distributions and the Central Limit Theorem

terms.def: The statistic <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>χ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>E</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mi>E</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\chi^2 = \sum \frac{(O - E)^2}{E}</annotation></semantics></math>, added over every cell of a table of observed (<math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O</annotation></semantics></math>) and expected (<math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math>) counts. It is 0 when the observed counts match the expected counts exactly and grows as they move apart.
terms.topicTitle: Setting Up a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence

terms.def: One cell's term <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>E</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mi>E</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{(O - E)^2}{E}</annotation></semantics></math> in the chi-square statistic. The cells with the largest components show where the observed counts differ most from what the null hypothesis predicts.
terms.topicTitle: Carrying Out a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence

terms.def: A family of right-skewed density curves for values of 0 or more, one for each number of degrees of freedom; its mean is the df. If <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_0</annotation></semantics></math> is true and the conditions hold, the <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>χ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\chi^2</annotation></semantics></math> statistic approximately follows one.
terms.topicTitle: Carrying Out a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence

terms.def: A chi-square test of whether one categorical variable has the same distribution in several populations or treatment groups, using separate random samples or randomly assigned groups. <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_0</annotation></semantics></math>: the distributions are the same.
terms.topicTitle: Setting Up a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence

terms.def: A chi-square test of whether two categorical variables are associated in a population, using one random sample classified by both variables. <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_0</annotation></semantics></math>: there is no association between the variables.
terms.topicTitle: Setting Up a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence

terms.def: A cluster sample splits the population into groups (clusters), chooses some clusters at random, and measures every individual in the chosen clusters.
terms.topicTitle: Random Sampling

terms.def: The coefficient of determination, <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r^2</annotation></semantics></math>: the fraction of the variation in the response variable that is accounted for by the least-squares line using the explanatory variable.
terms.topicTitle: Least-Squares Regression

terms.def: The number of ways to choose k items from n when order does not matter: <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_nC_k</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac linethickness="0"><mi>n</mi><mi>k</mi></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \binom{n}{k}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>!</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>!</mo><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>!</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{n!}{k!\,(n - k)!}</annotation></semantics></math>, read "n choose k".
terms.topicTitle: Factorials and Combinations

terms.def: The complement of an event A, written <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mi>c</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^c</annotation></semantics></math>, is the event that A does not happen. The complement rule: <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mi>c</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Introduction to Probability

terms.def: An experimental design in which every experimental unit is assigned to a treatment at random, with no grouping first.
terms.topicTitle: Experimental Design

terms.def: When sampling without replacement, the sample size is at most 10% of the population size. Then the selections are close to independent and the standard deviation formula for a statistic is accurate.
terms.topicTitle: Sampling Distributions for Sample Proportions

terms.def: The conditional probability of A given B, written <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>|</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(A \mid B)</annotation></semantics></math>, is the probability that A happens when we know B has happened: <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>|</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>∩</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}</annotation></semantics></math>. In a two-way table it is a cell divided by the total of the row or column for B.
terms.topicTitle: Conditional Probability

terms.def: A conditional relative frequency is a cell count divided by the total of its row or column: the share of one group that falls in a category, such as the share of first-time visitors who hiked. The shares for one group form its conditional distribution and add to 1.
terms.topicTitle: Summary Statistics for Two Categorical Variables

terms.def: What must be true for an inference method to work, checked in words with numbers: random (a random sample or random assignment), 10% (when sampling without replacement), and a shape condition such as large counts.
terms.topicTitle: Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion

terms.def: A range of values for a parameter, built as statistic ± (critical value)(standard error). For one proportion, the one-sample z interval is <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">^</mo></mover><mo>±</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><msqrt><mfrac><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p} \pm z^*\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})}{n}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion

terms.def: The success rate of the method that builds a confidence interval: for 95% confidence, about 95% of intervals built from many random samples capture the parameter. It sets the critical value.
terms.topicTitle: Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion

terms.def: A confounding variable is related to both the explanatory and the response variable, so its effect on the response cannot be separated from the explanatory variable’s effect.
terms.topicTitle: The Investigative Question Revisited and Data Collection

terms.def: For two-sample t procedures, the smaller of <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_1 - 1</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_2 - 1</annotation></semantics></math>. It never exceeds the technology (Welch) degrees of freedom, so it gives a slightly larger <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t^*</annotation></semantics></math>: a wider interval and a larger p-value. Both choices are accepted.
terms.topicTitle: Constructing a Confidence Interval for the Difference Between Two Population Means

terms.def: A quantitative variable that can take any value in an interval, usually a measurement such as time, length or weight.
terms.topicTitle: Variables

terms.def: A group that receives no treatment, a placebo or the standard treatment, to compare with the treatment group. A placebo is a fake treatment; the placebo effect is a response to it caused by expectation.
terms.topicTitle: Experimental Design

terms.def: A convenience sample is made of individuals who are easy to reach, such as shoppers at one store. It is not random and is usually biased.
terms.topicTitle: Potential Problems with Sampling

terms.def: The wording for a conclusion that the data support a claim about a parameter, as in "the interval gives convincing evidence that the true proportion is greater than 0.60". Evidence is never proof.
terms.topicTitle: Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion

terms.def: The correlation coefficient <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>y</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r = \frac{1}{n - 1}\sum z_x z_y</annotation></semantics></math>: a number from <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1</annotation></semantics></math> to 1 that measures the direction and strength of the linear association between two quantitative variables. It has no units and is not resistant to outliers.
terms.topicTitle: Correlation

terms.def: The multiplier <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z^*</annotation></semantics></math> in a confidence interval: the standard normal value with the confidence level's area between <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-z^*</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z^*</annotation></semantics></math>. It is 1.645 for 90%, 1.96 for 95% and 2.576 for 99%.
terms.topicTitle: Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion

terms.def: A cumulative probability is the probability that a random variable is at most a given value, such as <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(X \le 3)</annotation></semantics></math>, found by adding the probabilities of every value up to and including that value.
terms.topicTitle: Introduction to Random Variables and Probability Distributions

terms.def: A graph that shows, for each value, the proportion of the data at or below that value (the relative frequencies added up from the left).
terms.topicTitle: Graphical Representations for One Quantitative Variable

terms.def: The values recorded for the individuals in a study: answers, counts or measurements.
terms.topicTitle: Introducing Statistics: What Can We Learn from Data?

terms.def: The number that picks out one member of a family of distributions. For a chi-square test on a two-way table, <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>df</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{df}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>rows</mtext><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>columns</mtext><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= (\text{rows} - 1)(\text{columns} - 1)</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Carrying Out a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence

terms.def: A density curve is a smooth curve that models a distribution: it is on or above the horizontal axis and has an area of exactly 1 under it. The area under the curve over an interval is the proportion of values, or the probability, in that interval.
terms.topicTitle: The Normal Distribution

terms.def: The statistic <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2</annotation></semantics></math> from two independent samples or groups. Its sampling distribution has mean <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_1 - \mu_2</annotation></semantics></math> and standard deviation <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mfrac></mrow></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and is approximately normal when each sample mean is.
terms.topicTitle: Sampling Distributions for the Difference Between Two Sample Means

terms.def: The statistic <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">^</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2</annotation></semantics></math>, one sample proportion minus another. Its sampling distribution has mean <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_1 - p_2</annotation></semantics></math> and, for independent samples, standard deviation <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mfrac></mrow></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{\frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Sampling Distributions for the Difference Between Sample Proportions

terms.def: The features used to describe a scatterplot. Direction: positive (both rise together), negative (one rises as the other falls) or none. Form: linear or curved. Strength: how closely the points follow the form.
terms.topicTitle: Graphical Representations Between Two Quantitative Variables

terms.def: A quantitative variable that takes separate values with gaps between them, usually a count.
terms.topicTitle: Variables

terms.def: The values a variable takes and how often it takes each value or range of values.
terms.topicTitle: Variables

terms.def: A graph of a quantitative variable that puts one dot above a number line for each value; repeated values stack up.
terms.topicTitle: Graphical Representations for One Quantitative Variable

terms.def: The empirical rule (68-95-99.7 rule): in a normal distribution about 68% of values lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean, about 95% within 2, and about 99.7% within 3.
terms.topicTitle: The Normal Distribution

terms.def: A statistic used to estimate a parameter, such as the sample proportion <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">^</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}</annotation></semantics></math> for the population proportion <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>. Its value from one sample is a point estimate.
terms.topicTitle: Estimators

terms.def: An event is a collection of outcomes from the sample space, such as "the sum of two dice is 8". Its probability is the chance that the outcome falls in that collection.
terms.topicTitle: Introduction to Probability

terms.def: The count a cell of a two-way table would have, on average, if the null hypothesis were true: <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mtext>row total</mtext><mo>×</mo><mtext>column total</mtext></mrow><mtext>grand total</mtext></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\text{row total} \times \text{column total}}{\text{grand total}}</annotation></semantics></math>. The observed count is the count in the data.
terms.topicTitle: Setting Up a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence

terms.def: The mean, or expected value, of a discrete random variable X is <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_X = E(X) = \sum x_i p_i</annotation></semantics></math>: each value times its probability, added up. It is the average value of X over very many repetitions of the chance process.
terms.topicTitle: Parameters of Random Variables

terms.def: A study in which the researcher deliberately imposes conditions on individuals and measures their responses.
terms.topicTitle: The Investigative Question Revisited and Data Collection

terms.def: The individual (person, animal, plant or object) to which a treatment is assigned in an experiment. Experimental units that are people are called subjects.
terms.topicTitle: Experimental Design

terms.def: The explanatory variable may help explain or predict changes in the response variable, the outcome being measured.
terms.topicTitle: The Investigative Question Revisited and Data Collection

terms.def: Using a regression line to predict for values of <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> outside the range of the data. Such predictions are unreliable because the pattern may not continue.
terms.topicTitle: Linear Regression Models

terms.def: For a whole number n, <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>!</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>×</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mo>⋯</mo><mo>×</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n! = n \times (n - 1) \times \cdots \times 2 \times 1</annotation></semantics></math>, the number of ways to put n different items in order. By definition <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>!</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0! = 1</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Factorials and Combinations

terms.def: The minimum, first quartile <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_1</annotation></semantics></math>, median, third quartile <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_3</annotation></semantics></math> and maximum of a data set. Together they split the ordered data into four quarters.
terms.topicTitle: Graphical Representations of Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

terms.def: A table that lists each category of a categorical variable with its frequency, the number of individuals in that category.
terms.topicTitle: Tabular Representation and Summary Statistics for One Categorical Variable

terms.def: A gap is a stretch of the number line with no values; a cluster is a bunch of values set apart from the rest by gaps.
terms.topicTitle: Descriptions for One Quantitative Variable Distributions

terms.def: A graph of a quantitative variable that groups values into equal-width bins on a number line, with touching bars whose heights are the counts or relative frequencies in each bin.
terms.topicTitle: Graphical Representations for One Quantitative Variable

terms.def: The hypothesized mean <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_0</annotation></semantics></math>: the value of the population mean stated by the null hypothesis <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>:</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_0: \mu = \mu_0</annotation></semantics></math>. It comes from the question (a claim, a standard, a past value), never from the sample.
terms.topicTitle: Setting Up a Test for a Population Mean or Population Mean Difference

terms.def: The real situation behind the numbers: who or what was studied and what was measured. Results are always stated in context.
terms.topicTitle: Introducing Statistics: What Can We Learn from Data?

terms.def: Two events are independent when knowing that one happened does not change the probability of the other: <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>|</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(A \mid B) = P(A)</annotation></semantics></math>. For independent events, <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>∩</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>⋅</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)</annotation></semantics></math>. Events that are not independent are dependent.
terms.topicTitle: Independent Events and Unions of Events

terms.def: Two samples where the individuals chosen for one have no link to those chosen for the other, such as separate random samples from two schools. Samples linked person to person, such as husbands and their own wives, are not independent samples.
terms.topicTitle: Sampling Distributions for the Difference Between Sample Proportions

terms.def: A point whose removal would change the least-squares line a lot. Points with <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> values far from <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{x}</annotation></semantics></math> have high leverage and are often influential; a point with a large residual is an outlier.
terms.topicTitle: Least-Squares Regression

terms.def: The interquartile range, <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>IQR</mtext><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1</annotation></semantics></math>: the spread of the middle half of the data. It is resistant.
terms.topicTitle: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

terms.def: The distance between the two ends of a confidence interval, twice the margin of error. For a t interval it is <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mfrac><mi>s</mi><msqrt><mi>n</mi></msqrt></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2t^*\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}</annotation></semantics></math>: it grows with the confidence level and with the variability, and shrinks as the sample size grows.
terms.topicTitle: Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for a Population Mean or Population Mean Difference

terms.def: A question that data can answer: it names the population, the variable, what to estimate (such as a proportion or a typical value) and whether the goal is to describe or to find a cause.
terms.topicTitle: The Investigative Question Revisited and Data Collection

terms.def: A value is an outlier if it is below <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>1.5</mn><mo>×</mo><mtext>IQR</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}</annotation></semantics></math> or above <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1.5</mn><mo>×</mo><mtext>IQR</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}</annotation></semantics></math> (the fences). Another rule flags values more than 2 standard deviations from the mean.
terms.topicTitle: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

terms.def: The joint event "A and B", written <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>∩</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A \cap B</annotation></semantics></math> (the intersection of A and B), happens when both A and B happen. Its probability is the joint probability <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>∩</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(A \cap B)</annotation></semantics></math>; in a two-way table it is one cell over the grand total.
terms.topicTitle: Mutually Exclusive Events

terms.def: A joint relative frequency is the count in one cell of a two-way table divided by the grand total: the share of all individuals who are in both categories, such as first visit and hiking.
terms.topicTitle: Summary Statistics for Two Categorical Variables

terms.def: The check that the sampling distribution of <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">^</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}</annotation></semantics></math> is approximately normal: at least 10 expected successes and 10 expected failures, <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>p</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">np \ge 10</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>≥</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n(1 - p) \ge 10</annotation></semantics></math> (some books use 5). It is never "<math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>30</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n \ge 30</annotation></semantics></math>" for proportions.
terms.topicTitle: Sampling Distributions for Sample Proportions

terms.def: The law of large numbers says that as a chance process is repeated more and more times, the proportion of trials with a given result gets closer and closer to its true probability.
terms.topicTitle: Estimating Probabilities Using Simulation

terms.def: The least-squares regression line, <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{y} = a + bx</annotation></semantics></math>: the line that makes the sum of the squared residuals as small as possible. Its slope is <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi><mfrac><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>x</mi></msub></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b = r\frac{s_y}{s_x}</annotation></semantics></math>, and it passes through <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\bar{x}, \bar{y})</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Least-Squares Regression

terms.def: How far a confidence interval reaches on each side of the point estimate: <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>ME</mtext><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>⋅</mo><mtext>SE</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{ME} = z^* \cdot \text{SE}</annotation></semantics></math>. A larger sample makes it smaller; a higher confidence level makes it larger.
terms.topicTitle: Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion

terms.def: A marginal relative frequency is a row or column total divided by the grand total: the share of all individuals in one category of one variable. Listed for every category, they form the marginal distribution of that variable.
terms.topicTitle: Summary Statistics for Two Categorical Variables

terms.def: A design in which units are put in pairs of similar units and chance decides which unit of each pair gets which treatment, or each unit receives both treatments in a random order.
terms.topicTitle: Experimental Design

terms.def: The sum of the values divided by how many there are: <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x_i}{n}</annotation></semantics></math> for a sample. It is not resistant.
terms.topicTitle: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

terms.def: A binomial random variable with parameters n and p has mean <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_X = np</annotation></semantics></math> and standard deviation <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_X = \sqrt{np(1 - p)}</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: The Binomial Distribution
aka: standard deviation of a binomial distribution

terms.def: The middle value of the ordered data, or the average of the two middle values when n is even. Half the data are at or below it. It is resistant.
terms.topicTitle: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

terms.def: The general multiplication rule finds the probability that two events both happen: <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>∩</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>⋅</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>|</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B \mid A)</annotation></semantics></math>. For two draws without replacement, the second probability is the one given the first draw.
terms.topicTitle: Conditional Probability

terms.def: Two events are mutually exclusive, or disjoint, when they have no outcomes in common, so they cannot happen together: <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>∩</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(A \cap B) = 0</annotation></semantics></math>. Then the probability that one or the other happens is <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(A) + P(B)</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Mutually Exclusive Events

terms.def: Nonresponse happens when individuals chosen for a sample cannot be reached or do not respond. If they differ from those who respond, the results are biased.
terms.topicTitle: Potential Problems with Sampling

terms.def: A normal distribution, written <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N(\mu, \sigma)</annotation></semantics></math>, has a symmetric, bell-shaped density curve centered at its mean <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math>, with standard deviation <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> setting its spread. It models many roughly symmetric, mound-shaped distributions.
terms.topicTitle: The Normal Distribution

terms.def: The shape condition for t procedures: the population is normal, or the sample size is at least 30, or a graph of the sample data (dotplot, boxplot, histogram) shows no strong skew and no outliers.
terms.topicTitle: Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Mean or Population Mean Difference

terms.def: The two claims a significance test weighs, both about a parameter. The null hypothesis <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_0</annotation></semantics></math> states a specific value (<math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p = p_0</annotation></semantics></math>); the alternative hypothesis <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_a</annotation></semantics></math> states what the study seeks evidence for (<math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo><</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p < p_0</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>></mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p > p_0</annotation></semantics></math> or <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>≠</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p \ne p_0</annotation></semantics></math>).
terms.topicTitle: Setting Up a Test for a Population Proportion

terms.def: The specific value of the parameter stated in the null hypothesis, written <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_0</annotation></semantics></math> for a proportion, as in <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>:</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.70</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_0: p = 0.70</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Setting Up a Test for a Population Proportion

terms.def: A study that records variables on individuals without imposing any condition on them. A retrospective study looks back at existing records; a prospective study follows individuals forward in time.
terms.topicTitle: The Investigative Question Revisited and Data Collection

terms.def: One individual that data describe, such as a person, an animal, an object or a day. Each row of a data table is one observational unit.
terms.topicTitle: Variables

terms.def: A confidence interval for a population mean when <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> is unknown: <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo>±</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mfrac><mi>s</mi><msqrt><mi>n</mi></msqrt></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{x} \pm t^*\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>df</mtext><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{df} = n - 1</annotation></semantics></math>. Conditions: random, 10%, normal/large sample.
terms.topicTitle: Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Mean or Population Mean Difference

terms.def: A significance test of <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>:</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_0: \mu = \mu_0</annotation></semantics></math> for a population mean when <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> is unknown, using the t distribution with <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n - 1</annotation></semantics></math> degrees of freedom. A paired t test is a one-sample t test on the differences of paired data, usually with <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_0: \mu_d = 0</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Setting Up a Test for a Population Mean or Population Mean Difference

terms.def: A one-sided alternative claims a direction (<math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo><</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p < p_0</annotation></semantics></math> or <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>></mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p > p_0</annotation></semantics></math>); a two-sided alternative claims only a change (<math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>≠</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p \ne p_0</annotation></semantics></math>). The research question, not the data, decides which.
terms.topicTitle: Setting Up a Test for a Population Proportion

terms.def: The agreed order for evaluating an expression: grouped terms (brackets, fraction bars, roots) first, then powers, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction.
terms.topicTitle: Formulas, Order of Operations and Square Roots

terms.def: A value that falls far from the overall pattern of a distribution. It should be investigated, not simply removed.
terms.topicTitle: Descriptions for One Quantitative Variable Distributions

terms.def: The probability, assuming the null hypothesis is true, of getting a statistic at least as extreme as the one observed, in the direction of the alternative. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
terms.topicTitle: p-Values

terms.def: Two measurements that belong together, on the same individual or on two matched individuals (before and after, left and right, twins). Analyze the differences as one sample; the parameter is the true mean difference <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_d</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Mean or Population Mean Difference

terms.def: A number that describes a population. It is usually unknown, because finding it needs data on every individual.
terms.topicTitle: Variables

terms.def: A part of a whole is the count in one group divided by the count in the whole group it belongs to, giving a number from 0 to 1.
terms.topicTitle: Fractions, Decimals and Percents

terms.def: A percent is a part out of 100: the decimal form of a part of a whole, multiplied by 100. For example, 0.75 is 75%.
terms.topicTitle: Fractions, Decimals and Percents

terms.def: The pth percentile is the value with p percent of the data at or below it.
terms.topicTitle: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

terms.def: A circle cut into slices, one per category, each slice sized by the category’s relative frequency. It needs categories that together make up one whole.
terms.topicTitle: Graphical Representations for One Categorical Variable

terms.def: A value inside a confidence interval: the data are consistent with it as the parameter's value. A plausible value is not proven; values outside the interval are not plausible at that confidence level.
terms.topicTitle: Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion

terms.def: The proportion of successes in two samples combined, <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_c</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{x_1 + x_2}{n_1 + n_2}</annotation></semantics></math>. A two-sample z test uses it because the null hypothesis says the two proportions are equal.
terms.topicTitle: Setting Up a Test for the Difference Between Two Population Proportions

terms.def: The whole group of individuals (people, animals or things) that a question is about.
terms.topicTitle: Introducing Statistics: What Can We Learn from Data?

terms.def: The mean of a whole population, written <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math> (mu). It is a parameter, estimated by the sample mean <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{x}</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

terms.def: The part of a whole population that falls in a category, written <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>. It is a parameter, usually unknown and estimated by <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">^</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Tabular Representation and Summary Statistics for One Categorical Variable

terms.def: The standard deviation of a whole population, written <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> (sigma). It is a parameter, estimated by the sample standard deviation <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

terms.def: The probability that a test rejects the null hypothesis when a specific alternative value is true, <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1 - \beta</annotation></semantics></math>. It increases with the sample size, with <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>, and with the distance between the true value and the null value.
terms.topicTitle: Potential Errors When Performing Tests

terms.def: Whether a difference is large enough to matter in context. A result can be statistically significant (0 outside the interval, or a small p-value) but practically unimportant, especially with very large samples. Judge it by comparing the plausible values in the interval with a meaningful threshold.
terms.topicTitle: Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for the Difference Between Two Population Means

terms.def: The probability of a result is the proportion of times it would happen in a very long series of repetitions of a chance process. It is a number from 0 (never happens) to 1 (always happens), and a simulation estimates it with the share of its trials.
terms.topicTitle: Estimating Probabilities Using Simulation

terms.def: The probability distribution of a random variable gives each of its possible values and the probability of each, as a table, a formula or a probability histogram. The probabilities are from 0 to 1 and add to 1.
terms.topicTitle: Introduction to Random Variables and Probability Distributions

terms.def: A variable whose values are numbers that measure or count an amount, so arithmetic with them makes sense.
terms.topicTitle: Variables

terms.def: The first quartile <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_1</annotation></semantics></math> is the median of the lower half of the ordered data and the third quartile <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_3</annotation></semantics></math> is the median of the upper half (the median itself is left out of both halves when n is odd).
terms.topicTitle: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

terms.def: Choosing individuals by a chance process, such as a random number generator, so that no one’s judgment decides who is chosen.
terms.topicTitle: Random Sampling

terms.def: Using a chance process to decide which experimental units receive which treatment, so that other variables are balanced between groups on average.
terms.topicTitle: Experimental Design

terms.def: A random variable is a numerical value that depends on the outcome of a chance process, such as the number of people in a randomly chosen car. It is named with a capital letter and defined in context.
terms.topicTitle: Introduction to Random Variables and Probability Distributions

terms.def: A randomized block design groups experimental units that are similar in a way expected to affect the response into blocks, then assigns treatments at random within each block.
terms.topicTitle: Experimental Design

terms.def: The maximum minus the minimum: a single number that measures spread. It is not resistant.
terms.topicTitle: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

terms.def: A line <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{y} = a + bx</annotation></semantics></math> that describes how a response variable <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> changes, on average, as an explanatory variable <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> changes. Its output <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">^</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{y}</annotation></semantics></math> (y-hat) is a predicted value of <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Linear Regression Models

terms.def: The decision in a significance test. Reject <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_0</annotation></semantics></math> when the p-value is less than <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>: there is convincing evidence for <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_a</annotation></semantics></math>. Fail to reject <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_0</annotation></semantics></math> when the p-value is greater than <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>: there is not convincing evidence for <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_a</annotation></semantics></math>. A test never accepts <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_0</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Carrying Out a Test for a Population Proportion

terms.def: A count divided by the total number of individuals: the part of the whole in one category, written as a decimal, fraction or percent.
terms.topicTitle: Tabular Representation and Summary Statistics for One Categorical Variable

terms.def: Where a value stands within its own distribution, measured by a percentile or a z-score, so values from different distributions can be compared.
terms.topicTitle: Comparisons of the Distributions for One Quantitative Variable

terms.def: Using enough experimental units in each treatment group that chance differences between units tend to average out.
terms.topicTitle: Experimental Design

terms.def: The difference between an observed value and the value a regression line predicts: residual <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">^</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= y - \hat{y}</annotation></semantics></math>. Positive when the point lies above the line, negative when below.
terms.topicTitle: Residuals

terms.def: A scatterplot of the residuals against the explanatory variable (or the predicted values). Random scatter around 0 means a linear model is appropriate; a curved pattern means it is not.
terms.topicTitle: Residuals

terms.def: A summary is resistant if extreme values barely change it. The median and IQR are resistant; the mean, standard deviation and range are not.
terms.topicTitle: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

terms.def: Response bias happens when answers do not reflect the truth, because of leading question wording, sensitive questions, or pressure from the interviewer or the setting.
terms.topicTitle: Potential Problems with Sampling

terms.def: The part of a population from which data are actually collected.
terms.topicTitle: Introducing Statistics: What Can We Learn from Data?

terms.def: The part of a sample that falls in a category, <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">^</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mtext>count in the category</mtext><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\text{count in the category}}{n}</annotation></semantics></math>, read "p-hat". It is a statistic.
terms.topicTitle: Tabular Representation and Summary Statistics for One Categorical Variable

terms.def: The sample space of a chance process is the list of all its possible outcomes. When those outcomes are equally likely, the probability of an event is its number of outcomes divided by the number in the sample space.
terms.topicTitle: Introduction to Probability

terms.def: A sample survey collects data by asking questions of a sample of individuals. It is an observational study.
terms.topicTitle: The Investigative Question Revisited and Data Collection

terms.def: The sampling distribution of a statistic is the distribution of the values it takes in all possible random samples of the same size from the same population. Its spread shows sampling variability: how much the statistic changes from sample to sample. For the sample mean, <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{\bar{x}} = \mu</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>σ</mi><msqrt><mi>n</mi></msqrt></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Sampling Distributions and the Central Limit Theorem

terms.def: The list of individuals from which a sample is actually chosen, such as a roster, a map or a list of addresses.
terms.topicTitle: Random Sampling

terms.def: A graph of two quantitative variables measured on the same individuals: one point per individual, with the explanatory variable on the horizontal axis and the response variable on the vertical axis.
terms.topicTitle: Graphical Representations Between Two Quantitative Variables

terms.def: A segmented bar chart has one bar for each group, split into the categories of the other variable by percent of that group, so every bar reaches 100%. A side-by-side bar chart puts those percents as separate bars next to each other; a mosaic plot is a segmented bar chart whose bar widths show the group sizes.
terms.topicTitle: Tabular and Graphical Representations for the Distributions of Two Categorical Variables

terms.def: The overall form of a quantitative distribution on a graph: whether it is symmetric or skewed, how many peaks it has, or whether it is level (uniform).
terms.topicTitle: Descriptions for One Quantitative Variable Distributions

terms.def: The standard of evidence <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> (alpha), chosen before the data are collected, often 0.05: how unlikely a result must be, if the null hypothesis is true, before the null hypothesis is doubted.
terms.topicTitle: Setting Up a Test for a Population Proportion

terms.def: A procedure that uses sample data to weigh the evidence against a null hypothesis about a parameter. For one proportion it is the one-sample z test for a proportion.
terms.topicTitle: Setting Up a Test for a Population Proportion

terms.def: A simple random sample (SRS) of size n is chosen so that every group of n individuals in the population has the same chance of being the sample.
terms.topicTitle: Random Sampling

terms.def: A simulation imitates a chance process using a model with the same chances, such as random digits, a coin or a die, and repeats it many times to estimate how often a result happens.
terms.topicTitle: Estimating Probabilities Using Simulation

terms.def: A distribution with a long tail on one side. It is skewed right when the tail stretches toward larger values, skewed left when the tail stretches toward smaller values.
terms.topicTitle: Descriptions for One Quantitative Variable Distributions

terms.def: The slope of a line <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = a + bx</annotation></semantics></math> is <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math>, the change in y for each one-unit increase in x. From two points, <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Lines: Slope and Intercept

terms.def: The square root of a nonnegative number <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math>, written <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msqrt><mi>a</mi></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{a}</annotation></semantics></math>, is the nonnegative number whose square is <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math>; for example <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msqrt><mn>0.25</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{0.25} = 0.5</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Formulas, Order of Operations and Square Roots

terms.def: A measure of the typical distance of the values from the mean: <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><msqrt><mfrac><mrow><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}}</annotation></semantics></math> for a sample. It is 0 only when every value is the same, and it is not resistant.
terms.topicTitle: Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

terms.term: standard deviation of a random variable
terms.def: The standard deviation of a discrete random variable X is <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>X</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_X</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \sqrt{\sum (x_i - \mu_X)^2 p_i}</annotation></semantics></math>. It measures how far the values of X typically are from the mean, in the units of X. Its square, before the square root, is the variance.
terms.topicTitle: Parameters of Random Variables

terms.def: The standard deviation of the residuals, <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><msqrt><mfrac><mrow><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">^</mo></mover><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \sqrt{\frac{\sum (y - \hat{y})^2}{n - 2}}</annotation></semantics></math>: the typical size of a prediction error, in the units of the response variable.
terms.topicTitle: Least-Squares Regression

terms.term: standard deviation of the sample mean
terms.def: The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean: <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>σ</mi><msqrt><mi>n</mi></msqrt></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}</annotation></semantics></math>, for random samples of size <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> that are less than 10% of the population. It measures how far sample means typically fall from <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Sampling Distributions for Sample Means

terms.term: standard deviation of the sample proportion
terms.def: The spread of the sampling distribution of the sample proportion: <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">^</mo></mover></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\hat{p}}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><msqrt><mfrac><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \sqrt{\frac{p(1 - p)}{n}}</annotation></semantics></math>, using the true proportion <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>. Four times the sample size halves it.
terms.topicTitle: Sampling Distributions for Sample Proportions

terms.def: An estimate of a statistic's standard deviation computed from the sample, used when the parameter in the formula is unknown. For a proportion's interval, <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>SE</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{SE}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><msqrt><mfrac><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})}{n}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion

terms.def: The standard normal distribution is the normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N(0, 1)</annotation></semantics></math>. Standardizing a value, <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow><mi>σ</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}</annotation></semantics></math>, turns any normal question into a standard normal one, answered by Table A or technology.
terms.topicTitle: The Normal Distribution

terms.def: A number that describes a sample. It changes from sample to sample and is used to estimate a parameter.
terms.topicTitle: Variables

terms.def: A difference between treatment groups is statistically significant when it is too large to be explained by the chance variation of random assignment alone.
terms.topicTitle: Experimental Design

terms.def: The science of collecting, summarizing and interpreting data to answer questions whose answers vary from one individual to another.
terms.topicTitle: Introducing Statistics: What Can We Learn from Data?

terms.def: A display of a quantitative variable that splits each value into a stem (its leading digits) and a leaf (its last digit), so every value is kept. It needs a key, such as 7 | 4 stands for 74.
terms.topicTitle: Graphical Representations for One Quantitative Variable

terms.def: A stratified random sample splits the population into strata, groups of similar individuals, and takes a simple random sample from each stratum.
terms.topicTitle: Random Sampling

terms.def: The symbol <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum</annotation></semantics></math> stands for "add up": <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum x_i</annotation></semantics></math> is the sum of all the values <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>…</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Formulas, Order of Operations and Square Roots

terms.def: A distribution whose left and right sides are roughly mirror images of each other around its center.
terms.topicTitle: Descriptions for One Quantitative Variable Distributions

terms.def: A systematic random sample chooses a random starting point in an ordered list and then takes every kth individual.
terms.topicTitle: Random Sampling

terms.def: A family of symmetric, bell-shaped density curves centered at 0, with heavier tails than the standard normal. Each is set by its degrees of freedom; as df grows, the t distribution approaches the standard normal. Its critical values are written <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t^*</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Mean or Population Mean Difference

terms.def: The standardized test statistic of a one-sample t test: <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>/</mo><msqrt><mi>n</mi></msqrt></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}}</annotation></semantics></math>, the number of standard errors between the sample mean and the hypothesized mean. Its p-value comes from the t distribution with <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n - 1</annotation></semantics></math> degrees of freedom.
terms.topicTitle: Carrying Out a Test for a Population Mean or Population Mean Difference

terms.def: A standardized measure of how far a sample statistic is from the null value: <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mtext>statistic</mtext><mo>−</mo><mtext>parameter</mtext></mrow><mtext>standard error of the statistic</mtext></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\text{statistic} - \text{parameter}}{\text{standard error of the statistic}}</annotation></semantics></math>. For one proportion, <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">^</mo></mover><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><msqrt><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>/</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msqrt></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1 - p_0)/n}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: p-Values

terms.def: A specific condition imposed on experimental units. A factor is an explanatory variable in an experiment; its levels are the values it is set to.
terms.topicTitle: Experimental Design

terms.def: A tree diagram shows a chance process in stages: branches for the first stage with their probabilities, then branches for the second stage with probabilities given the first. Multiplying along a path gives the probability of that path; adding paths gives the probability of an event.
terms.topicTitle: Conditional Probability

terms.def: One repetition of a chance process or of its simulation, such as one random pick of 4 council members or one set of 10 simulated free throws.
terms.topicTitle: Estimating Probabilities Using Simulation

terms.def: A confidence interval for the difference of two population means, <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_1 - \mu_2</annotation></semantics></math>, from two independent samples or randomized groups: <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>±</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mfrac></mrow></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) \pm t^*\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}</annotation></semantics></math>, with technology df or the conservative df.
terms.topicTitle: Constructing a Confidence Interval for the Difference Between Two Population Means

terms.def: The test statistic of a two-sample t test: <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mfrac></mrow></msqrt></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) - 0}{\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}}</annotation></semantics></math>, the observed difference in sample means measured in standard errors. Its p-value comes from a t distribution with technology df or the conservative df.
terms.topicTitle: Carrying Out a Test for the Difference Between Two Population Means

terms.def: A significance test of <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0</annotation></semantics></math> for two independent random samples or two randomly assigned groups, with <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_1</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_2</annotation></semantics></math> unknown. It uses <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_1</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_2</annotation></semantics></math> separately (no combined standard deviation) and the t distribution with technology or conservative df.
terms.topicTitle: Setting Up a Test for the Difference Between Two Population Means
